Wife and I are expecting our first in about 3 months. Found this article, but was wondering if there's anything else I should expect.

A birth of your own child is one of the most wonderful events you can experience although it may not feel like it at the time as there's so much going on. Whether stuff goes smoothly or stuff goes bad for either the baby or for the mother, the experience is a little like a wedding in so much as in it goes really quickly and you will only have chance to take a breather and reflect when it's all over. Try your best to keep calm and remember your main job is to support your partner (and in a birth room you'll probably be the most expendable person in there by a mile). No one needs to deal with a dude that's freaking out right by a woman giving birth.

Speaking from quite a personal perspective, I was surprised and saddened that I didn't feel an immediate bond with my baby. I was overcome with emotion but I didn't feel an emotional bond and I took that bad, I felt like something was wrong and it was my fault. My wife had to go to theatre after the birth and I sat next to my sleeping baby in the cot thinking "Who the fuck are you? I don't know you and yet here you are and I'm responsible". It took me over a month before I felt that love I expected to feel from the off. If this happens to you don't sweat it, you will get that bond for definite.

And sleep lots before, you won't get that much after (especially if you're doing the cool thing and not just letting the mum do all the nappy changes, feeding, and all the other baby care).

That's some great advice to keep in mind. Thanks!

(especially if you're doing the cool thing and not just letting the mum do all the nappy changes, feeding, and all the other baby care)

My wife's had enough to deal with over the past 6 months, believe me, but most of it has been directly related to carrying a child. She didn't have much morning sickness or late night food cravings. It's mainly been dealing with body changes, the baby kicking, trouble sleeping, and things like that. I can provide emotional support and make her life easier, but there's not much else that I've been able to do to help. When the baby comes, I almost feel excited because I'll be able to actually tangibly help out by changing, cleaning, feeding, etc.

Your new baby will cry, A LOT, like more crying than you may think you can handle. If you know your baby has been fed, changed, burped and checked over for injury and is physically ok but still crying just know that crying is a good thing. It lets you know that your child is breathing for one and it will strengthen their lungs a bit. It will frustrate you, if it gets to the point where you are gonna snap, then snap but put the bay down first and go outside or to the garage or where ever is a bit of solitude for you. DO NOT EVER TAKE IT OUT ON THE BABY!!! It may sound like a no brainer to say that but infants can push a person to thoughts they have never had and that is ok, its part of the process to becoming a certifiably crazy young parent. It will get better with time the first few months are the hardest. Also remember how crazy and borderline psychopathic the baby can make you and relieve mom when ever you can, she is going to be having an even harder time than you are. Other than that just know that its 18yrs ideally until you get to be "alone" again, enjoy that time, cause its not gonna last forever!!!!

Signed, Lucious_The_Limp crazy father of two young even crazier kiddos

When you leave the hospital, you will wonder if the doctor and nurses know what they're doing allowing you to leave with an hours old human. No matter how many parenting classes you've been to, or books you've read, the moment you first put your son or daughter into their car seat will be surreal.

I'm just hoping they give us the right baby at this point. With our healthcare provider (in the US), we only have one option for the hospital where she can deliver, and we have been underwhelmed with them so far. One time, she went to the ER with stomach pains and although she told everyone she saw that she was pregnant with stomach pain, the ultrasound tech asked her if she knew she was pregnant.

Another time, she was waiting for test results. 2 hours later, someone said she could go. When she asked about the results, they had no idea what she was talking about.

So yeah, not the highest level of confidence at this point.

When we had our daughter, the OB asked us if we could change hospitals three days before my wife was due. My wife is a planner, so this sent her into a spin. The hospital had just re-opened, and our daughter was the second child born there. It ended up being a great experience in the end. I guess I'm saying; don't get overly nervous if things don't go exactly as planned.

The first three months suck, sleep is a luxury and not something you're entitled to in any significant amounts. There's nothing you can do about it. The first time that the baby sleeps through the night you will wake up in a panic because, oh shit, what if the baby was crying and I didn't hear it? That's normal. Remember the sage wisdom to sleep when the baby sleeps

I actually miss the under 9 months or so stage. They're not as interesting or entertaining, but there's only three things wrong at any given time: need changed, need fed, need sleep. Barring any medical problems, that's it. If you make that mental checklist and do it in that order when the baby is crying, you'll be fine--unless the baby has colic, then it's just going to be what it is so maybe try different formulas. Don't forget the checklist. Live it, learn it, love it and you will keep your sanity.

Wife will need your help. That was especially true in my case because she was preeclamptic and medicated appropriately, plus she had a cesarean which results in damaged abdominal muscles. She felt awful and had a hard time moving, I had to do a lot of (figurative and literal) heavy lifting. After 6 weeks or so things will go back to normal--well, the new normal.

You mentioned the checklist. I think that's going to be important for me. I tend to want to solve problems, and I can see myself getting through checking for changing, food, temperature and becoming frustrated when the baby is just crying because of something I can't fix. And if my wife is asleep or passed out and it's all on me in that moment, ok I think I just found something else I'm nervous about. :|

Don't forget the checklist. Live it, learn it, love it and you will keep your sanity.
